newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch see two years of strong growth ahead.
newsitem.headline: Dutch see two years of strong growth ahead.

text.p: Dutch GDP growth will outpace the European Union average in 1997 and 1998, unemployment will fall further and the deficit will turn out well below the three percent EMU norm, according to a new set of official forecasts.

The government's Central Planning Bureau (CPB) said on Thursday Dutch gross domestic product would show real growth of three percent this year and 3.25 percent next year, compared with an EU average of 2.25 percent in 1997 and 2.5 in 1998.
Dutch economic growth had exceeded the EU average in every year but one since 1989, after a long period of underperformance in preceding years, the bureau noted.
Exports will drive the economy, it said, with exporters benefitting from growth of world trade and the guilder's recent depreciation against the dollar, sterling and the lira.
Over 100,000 jobs will be created both this year and next, with the standardised unemployment rate falling to about five percent of the labour force in 1998, the CPB predicted.

While other EU member states struggle to bring their public sector deficits below the three percent of GDP needed for economic and monetary union the Dutch deficit is set to fall to 2.3 percent in 1997 and 1.7 percent in 1998, the CPB said.
Public sector debt is projected to fall to 73.8 percent in 1997 and 71.9 percent in 1998 from 78.0 percent in 1996.
The planning bureau said exports had gradually been taking over as the engine for economic growth since the second half of 1996 when growth of consumer spending started to slow.
Last year had brought an exceptionally strong rise of 3.1 percent in the volume of consumer spending, almost twice as much as the rise in free disposable income.
This was partly due to rising prices for shares and houses which made consumers feel wealthier and less inclined to save.
The CPB said savings ratios were likely to fall again in 1997 and 1998 helping to keep growth of consumer spending at a steady 2.25 percent despite slower growth of disposable incomes.

Exports are expected to show volume growth of 5.75 percent in 1997 and 7.25 percent in 1998 as a 3.25 percent depreciation of the guilder helps Dutch exporters claw back market share lost as a result of the Dutch currency's appreciation in 1995.

However, the slightly weaker guilder will push up the price of imported goods leading to a temporary acceleration of consumer price inflation to around 2.75 percent in 1997, about one percentage point above the rate in neighbouring Germany.
Dutch inflation would probably slow down to a rate of two percent again in 1998, the CPB said.
Business production is projected to rise by around 3.25 percent in 1997 and 3.5 percent in 1998 and is expected to be accompanied by increased profitability.
Business investment, adjusted to exclude big projects which distort the underlying trend, is expected to rise by 6.75 percent this year and 7.25 percent next year.
